meta.title: Why The Next Phase of Crypto Is Bigger Than You Think w/ Blue Macellari
meta.speakers: Raoul Pal (host), Blue Macellari (Head of Digital Assets, T. Rowe Price)
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · institutional crypto infrastructure that survived FTX, crypto's liquidity stall since '10/10', stablecoin fragmentation as a UX problem, tokenization hype vs. reality, accelerating institutional adoption signals, and an AI-risk digression on identity, self-reporting, and a wargame that always goes nuclear

snapshot: Interview with Blue Macellari, who built T. Rowe Price's entire crypto-native infrastructure from scratch starting July 2022 — weeks before FTX collapsed — and came through it with zero counterparty or vendor exposure.

Crypto liquidity has stalled since an unexplained October event ('10/10'); Macellari says no one in the industry has a consensus explanation, and this cycle notably didn't produce the usual wave of forced liquidations/bankruptcies.
AI has pulled marginal risk capital away from crypto — she compares the marginal Solana buyer to the marginal SpaceX IPO buyer, both now chasing AI equity exposure instead.

Stablecoins are fragmenting across permissioned, open-source, and multi-chain rails, recreating the 'too many streaming services' problem — both speakers agree bad UX, not technology, is crypto's biggest adoption blocker.

Tokenization-as-a-service has gotten cheap and fast, which raises a sharper question: tokenizing illiquid assets (like real estate) doesn't create real liquidity, it just relabels the risk — and retail buyers don't actually want it despite constant industry pitching.

Institutional interest is accelerating fast: Macellari has done 15-20 board presentations on tokenization in the past 6 months (versus zero requests a year ago), and Robin Hood is pressuring both traditional finance and crypto-native platforms to move faster.

Extended AI-risk tangent: Macellari describes a 2021 attempt to get Amazon, Meta, LinkedIn, Microsoft, and Google to agree on a shared on-chain digital identity standard — all agreed on the problem, none would agree to interoperable credentials — plus concerns about AI labs' voluntary self-reporting and an AI wargame study where models defaulted to nuclear escalation.

themes.status: SURVIVED FTX WITH ZERO COUNTERPARTY EXPOSURE
themes.title: T. Rowe Price built its entire crypto-native stack from scratch six weeks before FTX collapsed — and it held
themes.lead: Macellari joined T. Rowe Price on July 31, 2022 to build a fully crypto-native operation (the only shared legacy system is Microsoft Outlook), and the pre-built risk architecture meant zero counterparty or vendor exposure when FTX and the wider 2022 daisy-chain of bankruptcies hit.
bullets: Background: trained economist, was at Lehman Brothers in London during its 2008 bankruptcy, then did emerging-market distressed debt at Elliott Management before discovering crypto in 2017 via a Bitcoin remittance to the US from Brazil that took 60 minutes instead of 5 days.

Quit a top-10 global private equity fund to launch a market-neutral crypto fund in 2018 (cross-exchange arbitrage and basis trades) — jokes she's 'the only person in crypto from the class of 2017 who's not either retired or in jail.'

T. Rowe Price (a $1.8T asset manager with a large 401k/retirement book) had T. Rowe and Fidelity 'stick it out' through the 2022 crypto winter while Goldman and JPMorgan built desks and then pulled the plug, partly because US bank regulation became far more hostile than asset-manager regulation.
By 2023 the internal desk was trading 20+ tokens; the pre-built architecture meant T. Rowe took price/market exposure to the crash but zero counterparty or vendor exposure through the FTX unwind.

Key post-FTX lesson she draws: the danger usually isn't your direct counterparty, it's your counterparty's counterparty — she cites Three Arrows Capital as 'everyone's biggest client, and nobody knew,' echoing Raoul's Long-Term Capital Management comparison from his own Goldman days.
Risk-discipline principle from her former Elliott CIO, which she says was the most important lesson she carried into crypto: 'the most expensive thing you can be in our business is rigid.'

quote.text: The most expensive thing you can be in our business is rigid.
quote.cite: — Blue Macellari, quoting her former Elliott Management CIO

names.name: T. Rowe Price (TROW)
names.blurb: $1.8T asset manager where Macellari built the entire digital-assets infrastructure from scratch starting July 2022; survived FTX with zero counterparty exposure.

themes.status: UNRESOLVED SINCE AN OCTOBER EVENT REFERRED TO AS '10/10'
themes.title: Crypto's liquidity has stalled since '10/10' — and neither speaker has a clean explanation why
themes.lead: Macellari says the industry still doesn't have a consensus explanation for whatever happened around '10/10,' but the more durable story is a comedown from an unsustainable run of positive regulatory news plus AI absorbing the marginal risk-capital buyer that used to go to crypto.
bullets: Macellari: 'I don't feel like we really understand as a community what happened 10/10' — she's heard many after-the-fact explanations but none that fully resolve it for her.

Notable contrast with past cycles: despite fund drawdowns and withdrawals, this time there was no mass wave of forced liquidations/bankruptcies surfacing — she reads this as a sign of real market maturity versus 2018 or 2022.

From the Bitcoin ETF launch through last summer, crypto was on what she calls a 'sugar high' of continuous unprecedented regulatory news (new SEC/CFTC leadership, SAB 121 rollback) — a pace she argues was never sustainable, so the current lull is partly a comedown, not a collapse.

AI has pulled the marginal crypto buyer's risk appetite into AI equities instead — her analogy: the marginal buyer of the SpaceX IPO is likely also a Solana holder, and that capital has been going to AI, not crypto, over the past year.

Raoul's framing: excess liquidity (liquidity growth above GDP growth) has been weak, so what liquidity does exist has concentrated almost entirely into AI, and 'price begets price' — momentum has stayed with AI equities rather than rotating back to crypto.

Both agree the underlying crypto thesis (stablecoins, RWA tokenization, agentic payments) is strong even while current trading activity is weak — Raoul frames crypto's addressable market as having gone 'from 8 billion people to infinite agents.'

quote.text: The TAM of crypto has gone from 8 billion people to infinite agents.

themes.watch: Neither speaker offers a firm explanation for what actually happened on '10/10' — it's presented explicitly as an open, unresolved question, not a settled diagnosis.

names.name: Solana (SOL)
names.blurb: Used as the analogy for crypto's marginal buyer — the same investor profile Macellari says is now the marginal buyer of AI-adjacent equity deals like SpaceX.

themes.status: FRAGMENTING ACROSS PERMISSIONED, OPEN-SOURCE, AND MULTI-CHAIN RAILS
themes.title: Stablecoins are recreating the 'too many streaming services' problem — and bad UX, not technology, is the real blocker
themes.lead: Competing coalitions building permissioned, open-source, and multi-chain stablecoin rails are fragmenting exactly the interoperability that made 'sending a dollar' the whole point — and both speakers agree crypto's historically terrible UX is the bigger adoption barrier than any of that.
bullets: Raoul flags the stablecoin market splitting into permissioned coalitions, open-source chains, and multi-chain deployments as actively undermining interoperability — market-share land-grabbing when, per Macellari, 'you'll all have market share, just let it grow.'

Macellari's cable-to-streaming analogy: stablecoins today feel like the early fragmented-streaming era — you remember a show exists, can't recall which of 12 services has it, cancel one, then have to resubscribe when it moves — and that experience won't drive mainstream adoption.

Self-deprecating admission of the UX problem: she describes spending until 3am on GitHub and Discord trying to recover $20 sent by mistake, and simply gave up — as a self-described 'scripted mom of three' who is unusually willing to try new tools, she says there's 'no path to adoption' for the average non-technical user under current UX.

Her prediction: the eventual stablecoin market leader will be whoever abstracts away the backend and bridging complexity entirely, the same way users don't think about which Wi-Fi network or OS a video call is running on.

Everybody who was going to get into crypto through code, or through pure hardcore determination, is already in — meaning further growth requires products built for people who won't tolerate friction, not more infrastructure for people who already will.

quote.text: Us crypto people are kings and queens of that — we've made the worst UX and UI in existence, and we still have it.

themes.title: Tokenization-as-a-service got cheap fast — which makes 'who are you actually tokenizing this for?' the real question
themes.lead: What used to cost roughly $15M and 2.5 years to tokenize can now be done almost instantly and cheaply, but Macellari warns the technology can't manufacture real liquidity in illiquid assets — it can only relabel the risk, and retail buyers don't actually want what's being pitched to them.
bullets: Tokenization-as-a-service has advanced so far that a process once costing roughly $15M and around 100 people over 2.5 years is now close to instant and cheap — which shifts the hard question from technology/ops to pure business strategy: who are you trying to reach, and what do they actually want?

Observed mismatch: 'I've never met a real estate guy who has not said I'm interested in tokenization. But I've never met a retail investor who really cares about buying tokens on a share of some illiquid building' — she worries the industry is using tokenization to offload assets it has run out of natural buyers for.

Core structural point: 'it brings greater accessibility and the illusion of greater liquidity, but it doesn't actually create liquidity where there is none' — putting a non-marketable, gated fund on a blockchain doesn't change its underlying redemption terms, it just wraps them.

Real risk case: repackaging a fund's economic interest into a synthetic secondary market without changing the underlying terms — especially if combined with leveraged/looped structures — creates a 'powder keg' of counterparty risk investors don't understand they've taken on.

Fund managers themselves may push back: private equity/alternatives PMs deliberately want zero daily mark-to-market and don't want an investor letter effectively 'stamped' to anyone who held a token for 30 seconds — that opacity is part of how those strategies work, not an oversight to be fixed.

What should tokenize, per Raoul: liquid, homogeneous assets and yield/fixed-income products, since blockchain is the fastest and most efficient way to transfer and custody those — not illiquid real estate as a first move.

quote.text: It brings greater accessibility and the illusion of greater liquidity, but it doesn't actually create liquidity where there is none.

themes.watch: Both speakers flag that mishandled tokenization (obscured terms, secondary markets, leveraged looping) is where this 'doesn't end well' — the risk is explicitly about execution and disclosure, not the underlying technology.

themes.status: BOARD-LEVEL INBOUND SHARPLY UP OVER THE LAST 6 MONTHS
themes.title: Institutional tokenization interest is accelerating fast — except among the commodity trading firms who'd benefit most
themes.lead: Macellari has gone from zero tokenization board requests to 15-20 presentations in six months, and Robin Hood is forcing both traditional finance and crypto-native platforms to move faster — but the multinational commodity trading firms with the clearest efficiency case have oddly not adopted stablecoin rails at all.
bullets: Macellari has done 15-20 board presentations on tokenization and stablecoins for large institutional clients in the past 6 months, versus having never been asked before that — inbound requests are arriving independently of each other across different boards.

Robin Hood is applying competitive pressure on both sides of the industry simultaneously — pushing traditional platforms and pushing crypto-native platforms like Coinbase (described as 'pretty slow for what should be a more nimble organization') to move faster.

Demographic signal: consistent study-after-study data shows younger users skew toward holding more digital assets than traditional mutual funds, and Robin Hood's user base is now maturing into marriage/retirement life stages, pushing the platform into territory historically owned by traditional wealth managers.

Even after a fund is tokenized, institutional buyers (not retail) still need to build out their own crypto rails before they can actually purchase it — Macellari cites ongoing work with Franklin Templeton's Sandy Kaul as an example of how slow but real this education process is.

Surprising laggard: multinational commodity trading firms with obvious efficiency cases for internal stablecoin cash management (getting capital unstuck across dozens of currencies and jurisdictions) reportedly aren't looking at it at all, per a friend who heads trading at a major commodities firm — despite Louis Dreyfus and other soft-commodity houses already using smart contracts for letters of credit since 2016-17.

Proposed explanation for the gap: sell-side banks make more money pitching multinational treasury desks currency options and FX products than they would pitching stablecoin efficiency that cannibalizes that revenue — 'there's always somebody being paid to recycle the capital in a different way.'
Brazil flagged as an unusually crypto-forward market that doesn't get enough credit for how far ahead it is on this front.

quote.text: The rate of innovation and speed of adoption that Robin Hood has been doing — Vlad has done an astonishing job there.

names.name: Robin Hood (HOOD)
names.blurb: Pressuring both traditional finance and crypto-native platforms to move faster on product innovation, per both speakers.

names.name: Coinbase (COIN)
names.blurb: Described as being pushed to move faster by Robin Hood's pace despite being the crypto-native incumbent.

names.name: Franklin Templeton (BEN)
names.blurb: Cited via Sandy Kaul's tokenized yield-product work as an example of slow-but-real institutional tokenization adoption.

themes.status: FLAGGED BY BOTH SPEAKERS, DIVERGING TEMPERAMENT ON HOW WORRIED TO BE
themes.title: A failed 2021 push for shared digital-ID standards, AI labs self-reporting their own 'breakouts,' and a wargame that always goes nuclear
themes.lead: Macellari describes trying to get Amazon, Meta, LinkedIn, Microsoft, and Google to agree on a shared on-chain digital identity standard back in 2021 — everyone agreed on the coming problem and predicted their own decade of lawsuits, then refused to agree on interoperable credentials anyway.
bullets: In 2021 Macellari convened senior people from Amazon, Meta, LinkedIn, Microsoft, and Google, warned them AI-driven fake content impersonating real people was coming and they'd 'get sued like the banks did after 2008 — and you'll be sued for a decade over this,' and every one of them agreed with the prediction.

Despite that agreement, none would commit to a shared credentialing standard — she quotes the response as Microsoft refusing to accept Amazon's credentials — leaving digital identity/provenance as a still-unsolved gap she says should be 'top of mind' given how central it now is to distinguishing real from AI-generated content.

She's uneasy about AI labs' voluntary self-reporting of safety incidents ('something's escaped the lab') as effectively the only disclosure mechanism in place, given there's currently no way to meaningfully regulate frontier AI development at a government level.

Cites an Imperial War College study run during the Iran conflict period, testing multiple AI models in war-game scenarios: roughly 9 out of 10 times, models escalated to nuclear weapons use within 3-4 steps as the 'optimal' outcome — and inputting explicit civilian-casualty costs didn't change that outcome.

Referenced comparison point: intelligence capability is compounding on something closer to Reed's Law than Metcalfe's Law, with efficiency of intelligence output described as doubling roughly every 5 months — framed as an unprecedented pace no government can regulate in time.

Temperament divide between the two speakers: Macellari (fixed-income/distressed-debt background) says her instinct trends toward worst-case ('the machines are going to kill us all' is, she jokes, where fixed-income people's minds go), while Raoul says he's more optimistic that 'normally the good outcome prevails' and has chosen to lean into the trend rather than resist it.

quote.text: So tell me AI is like a teenager without telling me it's a teenager.
quote.cite: — Blue Macellari, on AI labs' voluntary self-reporting of safety incidents

themes.watch: The Imperial War College wargame and the AI 'self-reporting' framing are both relayed from memory in conversation, without a named source or link in this interview — treat as directional claims pending independent verification.

takeaways.title: Track whether AI capital rotation reverses — that's the leading signal for crypto's marginal buyer coming back, more than any single crypto-specific catalyst.
Evaluate stablecoin/payments plays on backend-abstraction UX, not which chain or coalition they're built on — that's where the eventual winner separates from the pack.
Before backing any tokenization narrative, ask who the actual buyer is and whether liquidity is being created or just relabeled — the real estate/retail mismatch is the cautionary case.
Watch commodity/trading-firm stablecoin adoption as a laggard indicator — it hasn't happened yet despite an obvious efficiency case, and a breakout there would be a real signal.
Track whether any major tech platforms actually converge on shared digital-ID/provenance standards — as of 2021 they agreed on the problem but explicitly refused to agree on the standard.

risks: Single-guest interview; Macellari's employer, T. Rowe Price, has a direct commercial interest in the tokenization and institutional-crypto-adoption narrative she's describing.

Specific figures cited in conversation (T. Rowe's $1.8T AUM, '15-20 board presentations in 6 months,' the ~$15M/2.5-year historical tokenization cost) are self-reported and not independently verified in this brief.

The Imperial War College AI wargame study and the characterization of AI labs' self-reporting practices are both recalled from memory mid-conversation, with no named source, publication, or link given in the interview.
This is a long, free-flowing 63-minute conversation with frequent cross-talk between two speakers; auto-generated captions can misattribute short interjections.
